conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the scientific consensus and high-quality evidence (including a Phase III trial stopped for futility and a meta-analysis) show no evidence of benefit for CoQ10 in improving movement symptoms in Parkinson's disease, thereby rejecting the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
Based on the retrieved evidence, "no" is the well-supported conclusion, though the history is more nuanced than a simple negative.

**Early promising signals, later refuted:** A smaller Phase II trial (Shults et al., 2002) found preliminary evidence that CoQ10 at doses up to 1200 mg/day might slow functional decline in early Parkinson's disease, as measured by UPDRS scores (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/782965). This generated interest in CoQ10 as a potential disease-modifying or symptom-improving therapy.

**Definitive Phase III trial found no benefit:** However, the larger, more rigorous Phase III randomized, placebo-controlled trial by Beal and colleagues (published in JAMA Neurology) tested high-dosage CoQ10 (up to 2400 mg/day) in early Parkinson's disease patients and explicitly concluded "no evidence of benefit" — the trial was stopped early for futility (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409; also indexed at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/?dopt=Abstract).

**Meta-analysis confirms lack of efficacy:** A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling multiple randomized controlled trials evaluating CoQ10 in Parkinson's disease similarly concluded there was no significant improvement in motor symptoms or UPDRS scores, reinforcing that CoQ10 does not provide meaningful clinical benefit (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9).

**Conclusion:** The weight of evidence—particularly the large, definitive Phase III trial and subsequent meta-analysis—does not support CoQ10 as an effective treatment for improving movement/motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. While an earlier Phase II study suggested possible benefit, this was not confirmed and was effectively overturned by higher-quality, larger trials. The scientific consensus, based on the best available evidence, aligns with the "no" answer to this question.
